image.alt: The well-defined eye of Hurricane Simon lies just off Mexico’s Pacific coast. Some outer cloud bands of the spiraling storm extend over land.

title: NASA satellites capture atmospheric gravity waves from Hurricane Simon
excerpt: The NOAA-21 satellite recorded ripples in the mesosphere caused by the category 4 hurricane off the Mexican coast.
bodyHtml:
NASA reported on October 14, 2026, that satellites observed atmospheric gravity waves generated by Hurricane Simon. The storm passed near the Mexican coast as a category 4 hurricane on October 11, 2026, with sustained winds reaching 250 kilometers per hour.

Data from the VIIRS instrument on the NOAA-21 satellite captured the gravity waves in the mesosphere during the early morning hours of October 11, 2026. These ripples form when latent heat released near the tropical cyclone’s eyewall drives strong convection, building tall cumulonimbus clouds with updrafts that can send waves into the stratosphere and mesosphere. The VIIRS day-night band is sensitive to airglow, which is faint light emitted by gases at those high altitudes.

The National Hurricane Center noted that the storm's inner core was brushing up against the coast, while the topography of the Sierra Madre mountains appeared to temper the storm’s intensity somewhat. As of October 13, 2026, forecasts of Simon’s intensity and path remained very low confidence.
topic: Hurricane Simon Lurks Off the Mexican Coast
